text: Concept in 60 seconds: Basic structure doctrine In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a 13-judge bench held, by 7 to 6, that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure. Why it matters. It is the main limit on Article 368, and the reason courts can strike down constitutional amendments. Remember. The Court never listed the basic structure in full. Later cases added items such as judicial review, free and fair elections and federalism.

Concept in 60 seconds: Article 21 Article 21 says no person can be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) the Court said that procedure must be fair, just and reasonable. Why it matters. This one article now covers dignity, livelihood (Olga Tellis, 1985) and privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017). Remember. Article 21A, the right to education for ages 6 to 14, was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

Concept in 60 seconds: Money Bill A Money Bill deals only with the matters listed in Article 110, such as taxes and government borrowing. It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha, and the Speaker certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill. Why it matters. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes, within 14 days. The Lok Sabha may accept or reject them. Remember. A Money Bill is different from a Financial Bill. The Aadhaar Act 2016 was passed as a Money Bill, and the Supreme Court upheld that in 2018.

Concept in 60 seconds: Anti-defection law The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment in 1985, disqualifies a legislator who voluntarily gives up party membership or defies the party whip on a vote. The Speaker or Chairman decides. Why it matters. In Kihoto Hollohan (1992) the Court held that these decisions can be reviewed by the courts. Remember. The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the one-third split exception. A merger now needs two-thirds of the party's legislators.

Concept in 60 seconds: Writs Article 32 lets you go straight to the Supreme Court for a Fundamental Right. Dr Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution. Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for other legal rights. Why it matters. Know the five: habeas corpus (produce the person), mandamus (perform a public duty), prohibition (stop a lower court), certiorari (quash its order), quo warranto (by what authority do you hold this office). Remember. The High Court's writ power is wider than the Supreme Court's.

Concept in 60 seconds: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles Fundamental Rights (Part III) can be enforced in court. Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36 to 51) cannot, as Article 37 says. Why it matters. In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Court said Fundamental Rights prevail. In Minerva Mills (1980) it said the Constitution rests on a balance between the two. Remember. Directive Principles guide the State. They are not rights you can sue for.

Concept in 60 seconds: Repo rate and the MPC The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to banks. A higher repo rate makes loans costlier and cools demand and inflation. Why it matters. Rate decisions are taken by the six-member Monetary Policy Committee: three from the RBI, including the Governor, and three external members appointed by the government. The Governor has a casting vote in a tie. Remember. The government has set an inflation target of 4 percent with a band of 2 percent on either side.

Concept in 60 seconds: Fiscal deficit Fiscal deficit is total government expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing. In plain words, it is how much the government must borrow in a year. Why it matters. The FRBM Act 2003 set rules to bring it down and keep it low. Remember. Primary deficit is the fiscal deficit minus interest payments.

Concept in 60 seconds: El Nino and La Nina El Nino is a warming of surface water in the central and eastern Pacific. It usually weakens the Indian summer monsoon and raises the risk of drought. Why it matters. La Nina is the opposite, a cooling, and is usually good for monsoon rain. Remember. A positive Indian Ocean Dipole, with a warmer western Indian Ocean, can offset the effect of El Nino.

Concept in 60 seconds: Zero Hour Zero Hour is the time right after Question Hour when members raise urgent matters without prior notice. Why it matters. It is not in the rules of procedure. It began in the Lok Sabha around 1962 as a convention. Remember. Question Hour is the first hour of the sitting. Zero Hour follows at about noon.

Concept in 60 seconds: The Preamble The Preamble describes India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic. The words socialist, secular and integrity were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976. Why it matters. In Berubari Union (1960) the Court said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution. In Kesavananda (1973) it said it is. Remember. The Preamble can be amended, but not in a way that changes the basic structure.

Concept in 60 seconds: President's Rule If a state government cannot be carried on according to the Constitution, the President can impose President's Rule under Article 356. Parliament must approve it within two months. Why it matters. It lasts six months and can be extended to a maximum of three years, with approval every six months. Remember. S R Bommai v. Union of India (1994) made the proclamation subject to judicial review and said a majority must be tested on the floor of the House.

Concept in 60 seconds: The Seventh Schedule The Seventh Schedule divides powers between the Centre and the states into three lists: Union, State and Concurrent. Parliament alone legislates on the Union List and states on the State List. Why it matters. Both can legislate on the Concurrent List, and if they conflict the Union law prevails (Article 254). Remember. Residuary powers, for subjects in no list, sit with Parliament (Article 248).

Concept in 60 seconds: Ordinances The President can issue an ordinance under Article 123 when Parliament is not in session. It has the force of an Act. Why it matters. It must be laid before Parliament and lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless it is approved earlier. Remember. D C Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) held that repeated re-promulgation of ordinances is unconstitutional. Governors have a similar power under Article 213.
